title: Dry Cleaning: Not Really Dry(!)
summary: Josh and Chuck explore dry cleaning, starting with the fact that it is not actually dry: clothes are cleaned in solvents rather than water. They cover early history (Thomas Jennings' 1821 patent, Jean Baptiste Jolie's camphene accident, flammable early solvents), the switch to carbon tetrachloride and trichloroethylene, and the adoption of perchloroethylene (perc) promoted by the One Hour Martinizing chain. They describe how dry cleaning machines recover solvent, the finishing process, stain treatment, and the health and environmental harms of perc, including EPA findings, Cape Cod contamination, California's ban, and cleanup costs. They close with alternatives to perc (wet cleaning, liquid CO2, hydrocarbon DF-2000, and Green Earth silicon-based solvent) and greenwashing concerns, followed by listener mail about Marie Tharp.

segments.title: Live show announcements
segments.summary: Hosts announce January 2024 live shows in Seattle (Paramount Theater) and San Francisco (SF Sketch Fest).

segments.title: Opening banter about dry cleaners
segments.summary: Hosts joke about martinizing and creases, and discuss how the pandemic and casual offices hurt dry cleaners.

segments.title: Personal dry cleaning stories and Korean American dry cleaner ownership
segments.summary: Josh recalls a friend's father's closet of dry-cleaned shirts. They note dry cleaner counts and that many owners are ethnic minority small business owners, many Korean Americans.

segments.title: Dry cleaning is not dry
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck explain that dry cleaning means no water is used, and that the storefront sends clothes to a separate facility.

segments.title: Thomas Jennings and early dry cleaning patent
segments.summary: Chuck describes Thomas Jennings, a Black tailor in New York City who received an 1821 patent for dry scouring; the patent was lost in an 1836 fire. Josh notes he was the first African American to receive a US patent and was recognized as a citizen through it.

segments.title: Jean Baptiste Jolie and flammable early solvents
segments.summary: Jolie, a dyer in France, accidentally found that spilled camphene cleaned a tablecloth. Early solvents such as kerosene, gasoline, and turpentine were flammable and dangerous.

segments.title: Shift to carbon tetrachloride, trichloroethylene, and perc
segments.summary: Dry cleaners moved to synthetic solvents carbon tetrachloride and trichloroethylene, which had serious health and equipment problems. They then settled on perchloroethylene (perc), which was safer and more effective.

segments.title: One Hour Martinizing and perc's rise
segments.summary: Chuck explains that perc allowed smaller storefront dry cleaning and that a chemist started One Hour Martinizing shops, which could return clothes in an hour with on-site facilities. Hosts joke about the name and note early workers' health complaints.

segments.title: Transition before break
segments.summary: Brief tangent about a TV show, then the hosts set up the explanation of what happens when clothes are dropped off.

segments.title: Dropping off clothes and inspection
segments.summary: Staff inspect garments and write down existing damage and stains to protect against later complaints. Stains are noted and pre-treated.

segments.title: Dry-to-dry machines and solvent recovery
segments.summary: Machines use perc in a closed drum that washes and dries in one unit. Fifth generation machines recover nearly all solvent, filter it, separate water, and condense vapor, with refills only every few years.

segments.title: Quality control and stain removal by hand
segments.summary: Hosts discuss human quality control, dirty filters causing dingy clothes and dye problems, and post-spotting by hand for stains that machines miss. Stains are classed as wet-side or dry-side, requiring different solvents or enzyme treatments.

segments.title: Home stain treatment and Shout
segments.summary: Hosts advise that customers should tell the dry cleaner about stains and discuss home pre-treatment, with the Smithsonian as a reference. Chuck praises Shout and its online stain guide. Some stains are permanent.

segments.title: Pressing and finishing process
segments.summary: Finishing uses shirt bucks that puff with steam and air, then ironing presses or human ironers. Chinos and cotton pants are hardest to press. Dry cleaning solvents penetrate fabric less than water, which reduces shrinkage.

segments.title: Plastic bags and home garment care
segments.summary: Hosts discuss plastic covers used on dry-cleaned clothes, advising removal and recycling at home, and the harm of storing clothes in them. Also brief laundering comparisons.

segments.title: Perc use statistics and EPA regulation
segments.summary: About 60 to 65 percent of US dry cleaners use perc, around 85 percent in Europe. EU countries mandate fifth generation machines. US rules limit new installations to fifth generation machines.

segments.title: Perc health hazards and Cape Cod study
segments.summary: Perc is a neurotoxin and carcinogen that moves through soil and groundwater and vapor. An EPA study of Cape Cod communities linked prolonged perc exposure to pregnancy issues, bipolar disorder, PTSD, vision problems and some cancers, though not all attributed solely to perc.

segments.title: Perc bans and cleanup costs
segments.summary: EPA set deadlines, and California banned perc as of 2023. Former dry cleaning sites are contaminated, with cleanup costing millions and owners held liable even when sites were previously permitted. Estimates place the US cleanup cost near eight billion dollars.

segments.title: Green dry cleaning and wet cleaning
segments.summary: Four green dry cleaning methods are introduced. Wet cleaning uses water and mild detergents; King County in Washington offers grants covering roughly forty to sixty thousand dollars for switching.

segments.title: Liquid CO2 and DF-2000 hydrocarbon solvent
segments.summary: Liquid CO2 machines cost about 150,000 dollars each and use captured industrial CO2. DF-2000, a petroleum-based hydrocarbon solvent from Exxon Mobil, is marketed as organic, which the hosts call a possible greenwashing term.

segments.title: Green Earth silicone solvent
segments.summary: Green Earth uses liquid silicone, which is inert and odorless. Silicone is reported to release dioxin during production, and a siloxane has been shown to be carcinogenic in rats, so its safety is uncertain. The hosts conclude liquid CO2 seems greenest but is costly.

segments.title: Josh's rug cleaning experience
segments.summary: Josh describes a rug sent out to a facility that came back with a sour wet smell and a stain not fully removed.

segments.title: Listener mail: Marie Tharp
segments.summary: Natalie, a paleoclimatology postdoc, writes that Marie Tharp mapped the Atlantic seafloor and was underacknowledged; the hosts say they will consider an episode on Tharp and Thomas Jennings.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact info
segments.summary: Hosts give the email address for listener mail and sign off.
